analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to safeguard personal data and notify breach victims; preempts stricter state data-security laws.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Data Accountability and Trust Act, the first breach-notification bill of the 114th Congress, never advanced past referral to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any company handling Americans' personal information to keep a written security program, and to tell breach victims and the FTC within 45 days when their data is stolen, along with two years of free credit monitoring or credit reports. It would have imposed stricter rules on commercial data brokers, including letting people see and correct their files and banning the buying of data under false pretenses. It would also have overridden state data-breach laws with this single national standard, and the House never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose personal data is stolen would get notice within 45 days plus free quarterly credit reports or credit monitoring for two years. People whose information sits in commercial databases would gain the right to see their file once a year for free, dispute errors, and stop marketing uses, and the bill would ban data brokers from obtaining information by false pretenses.

how_it_helps.text: Any company holding Americans' personal information would have to adopt a written security program, monitor for breaches, and securely destroy old data, under FTC rules considering company size, current safeguards, and cost.
Victims of a breach would get notice within 45 days and free quarterly credit reports or credit monitoring for two years from the breaching company.

Data brokers would have to let individuals review and correct their records once a year for free, keep audit logs of who accessed data, and would be barred from obtaining personal information by false pretenses.
State attorneys general could sue violators for civil penalties of up to $11,000 per day or per missed notification, and the FTC could enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Any business that holds customers' personal information would pay to build security programs, notify breach victims within 45 days, and provide free credit reports or monitoring for two years after a breach. Information brokers would face extra costs: FTC audits after a breach, procedures to keep records accurate, audit logs of who accessed data, and penalties for buying data under false pretenses.

drawbacks.text: The bill supersedes state information-security and breach-notification laws, so consumers in states with stricter rules — such as California's — could end up with weaker federal protections instead.

Except for state attorneys general, no one could sue under the act, and penalties are capped at $5 million for all notification violations from a single breach, leaving enforcement almost entirely to the FTC.

A company could skip notifying victims if it decides there is no reasonable risk of harm, and encrypted data gets a presumption of no risk — determinations made by the company itself, with FTC rules to define the carve-outs later.
Service providers that transmit, route, or temporarily store data are exempt from the security requirements, limiting coverage of the online economy.
Businesses, especially smaller ones, would bear compliance costs, breach notification expenses, and two years of free credit monitoring for each affected customer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, concrete gains to breach victims — timely notice, two years of free credit monitoring, and for the first time a federal right to see and correct data-broker files. But it carried a significant trade: by preempting state breach laws, capping penalties, barring private lawsuits, and letting companies self-certify that a breach posed no risk, it would have replaced some stronger state protections with a federal floor set partly on industry's terms. An honest supporter would call it a genuine first federal breach standard bought at the price of weakening state-level remedies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 28, 2015 and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
Two days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, where no further action was recorded.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
Its four cosponsors included one Republican and three Democrats, and the original sponsorship was bipartisan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that hold personal data and the data-broker industry are better off, because no federal security or notification standard was imposed and no single national rule replaced the state laws. Consumers also kept their stronger state breach laws instead of being preempted, but got no nationwide federal protection instead.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the five original sponsors split 4 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the bill never reached a floor test that would show where each party stood.

industries.note: The bill imposes new duties on data brokers — accuracy procedures, consumer access, audit logs, post-breach FTC audits, and a ban on pretexting — but its federal preemption would override stricter state rules governing them and bars private lawsuits premised on the act.

industries.industry: Companies holding customer data (retailers, banks, healthcare, tech)
industries.note: They would bear security, notification, and two-year free credit monitoring costs after breaches, but gain a single national standard in place of a patchwork of state laws, a $5 million penalty cap for a single breach, and no consumer right to sue.
Breached companies would have to provide victims two years of free credit reports or monitoring from the bureaus, creating demand for their paid services even as they must give the reports away.

Telecom and internet service providers are exempted from the security requirements for data merely transmitted or stored in transit, and their breach duty is limited to notifying the customer whose network they carry.
